title: dedicated-ghostload-investigation-scratch
content:
Summary:

Quick notes and rough runbook draft after two nights of tail-latency oscillations in dedicated GPU pools (west-1). Symptoms didn't look like classic noisy-tenant saturation; instead we observed short, repeated micro-spikes in GPU memory accounting and kernel stalls — we've started calling this pattern 'ghostload'. This is a work-in-progress capture of telemetry, immediate mitigations we tried, hypotheses, and concrete runbook stubs for oncall. Treat as messy; will tidy for postmortem.

What happened (high-level):
- Timeline (all times UTC):
  - 2024-11-02 22:40: first alerts: per-pool p95 inference latency up ~2.2x for ~5m windows across several dedicated pools in west-1.
  - 2024-11-02 22:45: SRE pager routed; initial snapshot showed overall GPU utilization at 45% but memory usage jumping in 10-20s bursts on 1-3 GPUs in the 8-node pool.
  - 2024-11-02 22:48: observed allocation churn spikes in allocator metrics (alloc/release ratio jumped x3).
  - 2024-11-02 22:55: autoscaler attempted a scale-up but canceled due to capacity-check mismatch (scale signal timed out).
  - 2024-11-03 00:12: pattern recurred; team recorded an extended heap of micro-spikes until we applied temporary evict policy and drained suspect compute nodes.

Key metrics pulled during incident (representative):
- p95 latency (pool-ded-w1): baseline 220ms -> spikes to 520-640ms during episodes.
- pod/gpu memory accounting (avg): baseline 5.1GB -> transient additions +1.2-2.3GB for ~8-25s.
- allocator ops/sec: baseline 34 -> bursts to 120.
- kernel stall rate (driver-reported stalls/min): baseline 0.2 -> 3.1 during spike windows.
- number of active backfills/ephemerals: increased from 2 to 7 for short windows.

Immediate mitigations tried (what we did, and why):
- applied temporary pool-level eviction window (shortened eviction grace from 120s -> 30s): reduced impact quickly but caused churn on lower-priority tenants.
- disabled a noncritical background warmup job (feature-flagged) that had recently been deployed to several customer configs (suspected correlation).
- forced drain of two nodes that showed highest spike counts; after drain, spikes moved to different nodes (indicates either allocator-wide behavior or client-side job pattern).
- raised autoscaler request timeout to give scale operations more time to complete; marginal effect.

Hypotheses (ranked, with evidence and tests):
1) Transient 'ghost' allocations from a client-side launch path (client retries/spawned allocs that immediately release) creating allocator thrash and kernel call churn.
   - Evidence: alloc/release ratio spike, many ephemeral containers reported in scheduler logs at the same timestamps, and correlation with a recent client SDK change flagged in linked ARTIFACTS.
   - Test: reproduce by running high-rate ephemeral start/stop loop on a staging pool; add additional allocation tracing.

2) Driver-level bookkeeping bug causing memory accounting to temporarily over-report (leads to false eviction triggers and kernel stalls).
   - Evidence: kernel stall rate rising; memory additions sometimes reported by driver but not matched by process-side memory.
   - Test: enable verbose driver debug on isolated host (low-risk window) and capture nvidia-smi/gpu top traces.

3) Autoscaler race condition where scale attempts overlap with heavy allocation churn causing scale cancellation and oscillation.
   - Evidence: scale operation canceled due to capacity-check timeout while allocator ops/sec were high.
   - Test: simulate high allocator ops with autoscaler in staging; add locking to capacity-check path to prevent double-cals.

4) A warmup/eviction interacting bug: warmup jobs grab caches briefly causing other tenants to mis-evaluate locality leading to hot-shifting of cache and causing extra KV cache misses (amplifies latency).
   - Evidence: disabling one warmup flag improved the window length; cache miss rates dipped slightly.
   - Test: instrument KV cache hit/miss with tenant tags and correlate with tenant allocation windows.

Runbook draft (for oncall handling ghostload pattern) — short checklist, prioritized actions:
- 0) Triage: check pool-health dashboard (p95, p99, alloc/release, node-evict-count, autoscaler-events).
- 1) If p95 > baseline * 2: flag incident, annotate slack channel with current span, and set pager escalation.
- 2) Snapshot artifacts: upload traces, allocator logs, kernel stall counters, and node-level nvidia-smi captures to incident ticket. Commands:
    - kubectl -n dedicated get pods -l pool=<pool> -o wide
    - curl -s http://metrics-host/api/v1/query?query=allocator_ops/sec > /tmp/alloc.json
    - ssh nodeX 'sudo nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY,UTIL > /tmp/gpu_dump.txt' (collect quickly, rotate after 10s)
- 3) Check ephemeral job heatmap: look for surge of short-lived pods (age < 30s) from same tenant/service.
- 4) Quick mitigation options (in order):
    A) Toggle warmup background job feature flag off for suspect tenant(s) if applicable.
    B) Apply temporary eviction window tightening at pool-level (short term). Note: communicate to affected lower-priority tenants.
    C) If sparks persist, drain the most affected node(s) (prefer nodes with highest kernel-stall counts) then monitor for redistribution.
- 5) Autoscaler steps: if scale-up canceled due to capacity-check timeout, increase the timeout and re-trigger. If repeated, disable autoscaler for pool and perform manual scale while reducing admission.
- 6) Communication: add incident note in #sre-dedicated with hypothesis tag and link to ticket; post brief customer-impact note to CS if any customers in affected pools are paying SLA.

Post-incident follow-ups / action items (owners and tentative due dates):
- Evan Park: generate synthetic workload that reproduces ghostload (due 2024-11-12).
- Ravi Iyer: instrument allocator with allocation stack traces for short-lived containers and push lightweight sampling to prod (due 2024-11-20).
- Maya Thompson (me): coordinate with product to identify which customers had warmup flags enabled and collect SDK version matrix (due 2024-11-10).
- Sofia Alvarez: create autoscaler simulation harness to test scale cancellation race and propose locking patch (PR linked in linked_artifacts) (due 2024-11-18).

Outstanding questions / unknowns:
- Are the micro memory spikes real allocations or driver bookkeeping artifacts?
- Why did drain move spikes (is the allocator state global or is there a shared client causing distributed spikes)?
- Is there any cross-region client behavior (e.g., a client hitting multiple pools in pattern) — we need tenant-level request traces.

Ideas for durable fixes (brainstorm):
- short-term: sample-enabled allocation tracing in prod for 1 week; automated rolling flags to disable heavy warmup sets when spike patterns detected.
- mid-term: change allocator to coalesce very short-lived allocations into a batched thin-alloc path to avoid kernel churn.
- long-term: implement a lightweight rate-limiter on ephemeral creation at scheduler level per-tenant with burst queueing and backpressure to client.

Notes to self / ops tips (less formal):
- When collecting nvidia-smi output, capture at 5s cadence for 30s; the spikes are short — 60s snapshots can miss them.
- Watch for allocator latency (p50 alloc latency) spikes rather than only ops/sec — kernel stalls often show up as alloc latency tail.
- Keep the eviction policy experiment in a toggle — it helps buy breathing room but can penalize noncritical tenants heavily.

References & logs:
- JIRA-SRE-2147 (investigation ticket)
- PR: allocator coalesce spike prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/allocator/pull/482
- Slack thread: #sre-dedicated (thread_ts=1709820300.000200)

Draft postmortem outline (what to include later):
1) Executive summary (what we saw, customer impact, duration).
2) Timeline with annotated graphs.
3) Root-cause analysis (finalized).
4) Contributing factors (autoscaler timeouts, warmup rollout, driver accounting oddities).
5) Immediate mitigations taken.
6) Long-term remediation plan (owners, timelines).
7) Lessons learned & runbook updates.

Open TODO for next oncall: add short-lived allocation sampling at 0.1% rate and ensure autotriggers create a trace in ticket when pattern matches definition: (alloc-releases/sec ratio > 2 and allocs avg age < 30s and kernel stall rate > 1).

-- End of scratch. Please add notes inline, update owners if overloaded, and if someone from product/dev thinks the warmup jobs are unrelated, record the counter-evidence here.
